planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in moist, acidic bottomland soil; Turnage 57 is unusually precocious for a mayhaw, often flowering and setting its first fruit the year after grafting, but it needs a different late-blooming mayhaw nearby to pollinate it since its own pollen is sterile.

directions: Turnage 57 was selected by Georgia growers for its late March bloom, a trait that helps the flowers dodge the hard late freezes that periodically wipe out crops on earlier-blooming mayhaw cultivars. The medium-sized fruit has bright red skin over orange flesh and ripens from late April into mid-May on a moderately vigorous tree with a distinctive semi-weeping branch habit. Because its own pollen is not viable, plant it alongside another late-season mayhaw such as Turnage 88 or Saline for dependable cross-pollination and fruit set. Expect a faster-than-average path to first harvest, with heavier crops building over the following several seasons.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in moist, acidic bottomland soil; Turnage 88 is a high-vigor selection that takes longer than most mayhaws to settle into heavy bearing, so give it a full season of establishment care before expecting a serious crop.

directions: Turnage 88 shares its late-March bloom window and sibling-like fruit — medium-sized, bright red-skinned, orange-fleshed — with the companion selection Turnage 57, but grows noticeably more vigorously and takes roughly eight years from planting to reach its full, very heavy production rather than bearing precociously. Once mature, trees are reliably productive growers describe as among the heaviest-cropping of the named western mayhaws. Plant with another late-blooming mayhaw cultivar for best pollination, and allow extra room for its larger eventual canopy compared with more compact selections. Harvest runs from late April into mid-May as the ground beneath the tree fills with dropped fruit.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in consistently moist to wet, acidic soil; Lindsey is a Louisiana-origin eastern mayhaw selection valued for ripening its crop in a tight window rather than trickling in over several weeks, which simplifies harvest.

directions: Lindsey is a named selection of eastern mayhaw (Crataegus aestivalis) prized by Louisiana growers for carrying noticeably larger, elongated red fruit than typical wild seedlings along with better-than-average resistance to the leaf and fruit diseases that trouble mayhaws in humid springs. Its crop ripens in a concentrated burst around the first week of May rather than dribbling in over a month, so most of the harvest can be gathered in one or two passes under the tree. It bears reliable annual crops once established, making it a dependable choice for anyone wanting consistent mayhaw jelly supply rather than a boom-and-bust yield. Site it in a low, wet spot or swale where the roots can stay consistently moist through spring.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in consistently moist, acidic bottomland soil; Lori is an eastern mayhaw selection bred to drop most of its crop within a short window, which suits growers who prefer to harvest in a single concentrated effort rather than making repeat trips under the tree.

directions: Lori is a named eastern mayhaw (Crataegus aestivalis) selection carrying small, elongated red fruit similar in shape to its sibling selection Lindsey, but distinguished by an especially synchronized ripening pattern — growers report roughly four-fifths of the crop reaching peak ripeness at essentially the same time in early May. That concentrated drop makes it practical to collect most of a season's fruit in one or two gathering sessions rather than returning to the tree repeatedly over several weeks. Like other mayhaws it thrives with wet feet, so plant it where spring rains pool or along a pond margin rather than in average garden soil. Cross-pollination with another mayhaw cultivar improves fruit set.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in moist to wet, acidic soil along a pond edge, bayou margin, or low swale; Reliable blooms later than many mayhaw cultivars, which helps its flowers escape the late cold snaps that can knock out an early-blooming tree's entire crop for the year.

directions: Reliable earns its name less from exceptional fruit quality than from year-to-year consistency, bearing a dependable crop of large red haws most seasons even when earlier-blooming mayhaws nearby lose their flowers to a late freeze. Left untrimmed it tends toward a large, multi-stemmed shrub rather than a single-trunked tree, though it can be trained to either form with early pruning. Like all mayhaws it sets heavier crops with a second cultivar nearby for cross-pollination, and the fruit is destined for the same jelly pot and syrup uses as other named selections. It's a sound choice for a grower who wants a backup late-season tree to hedge against spring frost losses on an early variety.
